newsitem.title: JORDAN: Egypt says Arab-Israeli peace process at low point.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says Arab-Israeli peace process at low point.

text.p: Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said on Tuesday Arab-Israeli peace negotiations had reached their lowest point in 20 years.

Moussa, stopping off in Amman on his way to a meeting of Arab foreign ministers in Syria, said Israel was undermining existing peace agreements with Arabs by abandoning the principle of swapping captured Arab land in return for peace.

"We have now arrived at a very bad moment when all of the achievements which have been painstakingly negotiated during the last several years are threatened," Moussa told a U.N.-sponsored workshop in Amman.
"The peace process has reached its lowest ebb since it started in 1977," Moussa said, referring to the year that Egypt's former President Anwar Sadat made a ground-breaking visit to Jerusalem.

"We have to be optimistic. But I am not," said Moussa, whose country has been trying to restart Israeli-Palestinian peace talks, frozen since Israel began building a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.
He said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu must suspend all settlement building on Arab land before progress could be made.
"We cannot talk while the bulldozers are working," he said.
Moussa also criticised Netanyahu's insistence on putting Israeli security ahead of efforts for peace.

"This proposition is founded on a facile assumption that the construction of overbearing security arrangements will suffice to contain the instability generated from not having addressed the core factors of conflict in the first place," he said.
Moussa, who held talks with Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali, was due in Syria later on Tuesday for a meeting of foreign ministers of Syria, Egypt and the six oil-rich Gulf states.

They are expected to discuss the fate of the peace talks and the formation of a common Arab market -- a direct snub to Israel which hoped its 1993 accord with Palestinians would pave the way for its integration into Arab economies.
